title: Intelligent Guesses Method
summary: Substitution method to verify asymptotic bounds using a reasonable assumption and an inductive proof. It includes when to use it, how to choose the assumption, how to close inequalities, how to fit base cases, and examples where other methods do not directly apply.

learningObjectives.text: Understand that the substitution method does not automatically discover the solution, but rather verifies a proposed bound.
Choose a reasonable assumption using tree intuition, comparison with previous methods or known patterns.
Test an upper bound using an inductive hypothesis of the form T(k) ≤ C·g(k).
Test a lower bound using an inductive hypothesis of the form T(k) ≥ c·g(k).
Close the inequality by choosing sufficiently large or sufficiently small constants.
Adjust the n₀ when the bound does not work in the first values, without altering the asymptotic conclusion.
Recognize when the simple assumption does not work and it is necessary to strengthen the inductive hypothesis.
Apply substitution to recurrences that do not fit cleanly into the Master Theorem, balanced tree, or characteristic equation.
Distinguish between intuiting an answer and demonstrating it formally by induction.

terms.label: Smart guess
terms.definition: Candidate bound for T(n), chosen by mathematical intuition, recursion tree, comparison with known cases or dominant behavior.

terms.label: Substitution method
terms.definition: Method that verifies a bound by substituting the inductive hypothesis within the recurrence.

terms.label: Inductive hypothesis
terms.definition: Temporary assumption that the bound already holds for inputs less than n, used to show that it also holds for n.

terms.label: Close the inequality
terms.definition: Ensure that the expression obtained after substituting is limited by the proposed form.

terms.label: Constant C
terms.definition: Positive constant chosen so that an upper bound O can absorb minor terms.

terms.label: Constant c (lower)
terms.definition: Positive constant used to demonstrate a lower bound Ω.

terms.label: n₀
terms.definition: Point from which the inductive limit begins to be fulfilled. Smaller values ​​can be treated as base cases.

terms.label: Strengthened hypothesis
terms.definition: More precise version of the proposed bound, used when the simple bound does not close with a positive residual term.

terms.label: O test
terms.definition: Proof that T(n) does not exceed a multiplicative constant of g(n) for sufficiently large n.

terms.label: Ω test
terms.definition: Proof that T(n) is at least a multiplicative constant of g(n) for sufficiently large n.

chapters.title: Intelligent Guesses Method
chapters.summary: Inductive verification of dimensions for recurrences through substitution.

learningObjectives.text: Identify when it is appropriate to use substitution to verify a solution.
Avoid presenting an assumption as a conclusion before proving it.

content.text: The Intelligent Guessing method, also called the substitution method, is used when you already have a reasonable candidate for the solution to a recurrence and need to formally verify it.

It is not a method to magically guess. First, an intuition is obtained with a recursion tree, comparison with known recurrences, sums by levels or growth patterns. The bound is then proven by induction.

content.text: The difficult part of the method is not substituting. The difficult part is choosing a level that has a real chance of closing. If you choose a dimension that is too small, the test fails. If you choose a dimension that is too large, it may close but be useless or imprecise.

blocks.title: When the test does not close

content.text: The fact that a test does not close does not automatically imply that the bound is false. Sometimes the bound is correct, but the inductive hypothesis is too weak. In those cases it is strengthened with a margin term.
